title: Quasilinear Equivalence Checking for Detector Error Models
abstract: A Detector Error Model (DEM) is a structured representation of error mechanisms in quantum circuits, which has gained popularity in quantum compilation pipelines for its ability to capture fault-tolerance at a circuit level. It lists error mechanisms as instructions targeting detectors and observables, specifying for each physical fault channel the probability that the fault fires, the detectors it triggers, and the observables it flips.   In this paper, we develop an equational theory for DEMs, with its associated categorical semantics. We present a sound, terminating, confluent rewriting system for DEM terms, formulating it as a symmetric monoidal theory (a PROP) over the Giry monad. We prove that every DEM term has a unique normal form, which can be computed efficiently in quasilinear time $O(k|E|\log|E|)$, where $|E|$ is the number of instructions and $k$ bounds the size of a target set. This provides a complete set of invariants (via Tanner graphs) for structural DEM equivalence. We provide the first static decision procedure for DEM equivalence, with rigorous correctness guarantees. It is complete (decides full decoder-equivalence exactly) for non-adaptive quantum error correction (QEC) pipelines, and scales to a sound and applicable decision procedure for partially-adaptive circuits (lattice surgery, distributed QEC, ...) without suffering exponential overhead. We discuss its application to the verification and optimisation of quantum compilers.
summary: This paper develops a formal, algebraic theory for Detector Error Models (DEMs), which are used to characterize noise in quantum circuits. It introduces an efficient rewriting system that guarantees a unique normal form for any DEM term. This allows researchers to create the first static decision procedure to rigorously check if two different error descriptions represent the same underlying physical fault model.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a complete, decidable mathematical theory for Detector Error Models (DEMs) to rigorously check if two different descriptions of quantum hardware noise are equivalent.
main_result: The authors provide an efficient quasilinear time decision procedure based on computing a unique normal form derived from the DEM structure via rewriting systems and Tanner graphs. This establishes structural equivalence for non-adaptive QEC pipelines and provides sound procedures for partially-adaptive circuits.
method: The methodology involves constructing an equational theory for DEMs, defining a confluent rewriting system (PROP), and characterizing equivalence by comparing unique normal forms derived from the structure's invariants (Tanner graphs).
model_or_system: The model is the Detector Error Model (DEM), which formally describes physical error mechanisms in quantum circuits. These errors are characterized by probabilities, specific detectors triggered, and logical observables flipped during a fault event.
key_observables: Detector outcomes ($\{0, 1\}^D$), observable outcomes ($\{0, 1\}^O$), and the associated probability distributions (scope distribution $\mu$).
important_parameters: Error probabilities ($p < 0.5$); circuit depth/size ($|E|$); scope structure (Skeleton $ho(t)$).
main_assumptions: The initial analysis assumes detector indices are absolute; later work addresses the limitations of assuming observable-separation for full decoder-equivalence in adaptive circuits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Tanner graph reduction, showing how error mechanisms with identical targets are fused algebraically using probability combination rules (e.g., $p_{12} = p_1 \oplus p_2$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the DEM structure and its algebraic theory to proving the existence of a unique normal form via rewriting systems, establishing invariants using Tanner graphs, and finally developing increasingly general decision procedures for equivalence (scope-local vs. full decoder-equivalence) applicable to adaptive QEC.
why_interesting: This work provides foundational mathematical tools for verifying quantum computation correctness by providing rigorous methods to compare complex noise models derived from physical hardware constraints.
